analysis.one_liner: Stops bankruptcy courts from erasing legal claims against companies and people who didn't file for bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill, filed in the final month of the 118th Congress, never left the Senate Judiciary Committee and received no hearing or vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company files for bankruptcy, its bankruptcy court can sometimes issue a 'nondebtor release' — an order that wipes out lawsuits not against the company itself, but against other parties, like a parent corporation or wealthy owners. This bill would ban courts from doing that unless the person holding the claim signs a clear, written agreement to give it up. It would also let judges throw out bankruptcy filings made through 'divisional mergers' that split a company's assets from its liabilities to dump lawsuits on a hollowed-out shell, and it would limit temporary court orders that pause those lawsuits to 90 days.
analysis.who_benefits: People holding legal claims against a company's parent or affiliates — for example mesothelioma victims, consumers, and workers injured by products — who today can see their lawsuits erased by a bankruptcy judge even though they never filed for bankruptcy and never agreed. It also helps creditors of the debtor, since assets can no longer be peeled off into a liability-free affiliate.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of corporate wrongdoing and creditors

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits a bankruptcy court from discharging, releasing, or enjoining claims or causes of action held by entities other than the debtor against parties other than the debtor, unless the claimholder expressly consents in a signed writing after clear notice, with no penalty for refusing to consent [S2].

It requires a bankruptcy court to dismiss a Chapter 11 case if the debtor's assets and liabilities were split apart in a divisional merger during the prior ten years with the intent or foreseeable effect of separating material assets from material liabilities [S2].

It caps temporary stays or injunctions of third-party claims in Chapter 11 cases at 90 days unless the claimholder consents, and gives courts of appeals jurisdiction over any such stays, with the stay dissolving 90 days after issuance unless affirmed [S2].
The bill applies to cases already pending at enactment, not just future filings, though it leaves already-final orders untouched [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, parent corporations, wealthy owners, and affiliates of bankrupt companies would pay — they could no longer use a subsidiary's bankruptcy filing to shed their own liability for defective products, toxic exposure, or other harms, and could no longer rely on the 'Texas two-step' strategy of splitting a company so lawsuits land on a shell entity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Parent corporations and wealthy owners of debtors

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the ban's opponents argue that some nondebtor releases let thousands of claimholders share in a settlement quickly — the mechanism the Supreme Court struck down in the Purdue Pharma case had distributed billions to opioid victims — so a hard ban can make complex mass-tort restructurings harder to settle and push cases into slower court battles [S2].

The bill's consent exception only accepts an express signed writing, not acceptance of a plan or silence, so claimholders who would have voted yes on a settlement plan now must separately sign off, adding friction to large restructurings [S2].

Mandatory dismissal of cases involving ten-year-old divisional mergers could unwind restructurings done long before the bankruptcy, raising costs and uncertainty even where no liability-shifting was intended [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core rule — no judge erases your lawsuit against a non-filing party unless you agree in writing — is a clear win for injured people and other claimholders, and the bill preserves consensual deals, court-appointed fiduciaries, and legitimate asset sales. The real cost falls on defendants with large liabilities and on the speed of complex settlements; critics can fairly argue that some mass-tort victims preferred the release-based deals that this bill would rule out, since those claimholders must now affirmatively consent for any release to stand.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 3, 2024, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on December 3, 2024, in the closing weeks of the 118th Congress [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; no further action appears in the record [S4].
Four senators — 3 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate Independents — cosponsored it; no Republicans did [S3].

The bill text targets the 'nondebtor release' practice the Supreme Court addressed in 2024 in the Purdue Pharma case, where a bankruptcy plan had shielded members of the Sackler family from opioid lawsuits, and also targets divisional mergers that separate assets from liabilities [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies and wealthy individuals facing mass lawsuits are better off, since the practice of using a subsidiary's bankruptcy to erase claims against them remains available; claimholders like injury victims gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that use bankruptcy to shed lawsuits

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 3, 2024 and became its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Sen. Dick Durbin, D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the four weeks it was pending; it died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent, and no Republican cosponsored.

industries.industry: Parent corporations and affiliates of bankrupt companies
industries.note: The bill removes the bankruptcy-court tool that lets a filing subsidiary shield its parent from lawsuits over injuries and defects. For claimholders, that protection is the point: the parent's gain has come directly out of victims' lawsuits.
The bill outlaws the divisional-merger restructuring strategy and most third-party releases and long stays, shrinking the toolkit available in complex Chapter 11 cases.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' attorneys and claimholders in mass torts
industries.note: Injury victims keep enforceable claims against non-filing parties unless they personally sign a consent, and mass-tort litigation against solvent parents survives a subsidiary's bankruptcy.
